references: Paul et al. (2019); Kääb et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: From 2004 to September 2007, the glacier advanced by about 300m before it collapsed again at some time between 23 September and 2 November 2007. Its maximum extent before the collapse was much smaller than in 2004, close to its "normal" minimum extent. This indicates that the surge/collapse mechanism might have been different, that lubrification by melt water might have played a role, or that the glacier has reached a different point of dynamic stability. It is well possible that after three years, the collapsed material was more a loose ice/rock mГ©lange rather than a homogenous glacier. A small part of the flat, lower glacier remained in its bed. This part is separated from highly crevassed dirty ice higher up that is still connected to the southern tributary. In other words, the rupture did not follow a potential failure zone, but occurred somewhere across the glacier.

triggers: Meltwater input; Weak bedrock material; Surge-like activity or surge-type glacier
references: Leinss et al. (2021); Kääb et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: Prior to its detachment, dp-19 had an active surge history. L5 imagery indicates a surge-like advance of about 230m between 1991 and 1995. The glacier advanced again by about 100 m between 1999 and 2003, followed by quiescence until 2006. All datasets indicate that the glacier’s slow retreat and melt continued until shortly before the detachment in 2019. About 3 weeks prior to the detachment, around 11 July 2019, the Bergschrund started widening by 1m per day, and we observed increased sliding leading to enhanced lateral crevassing around the detached area. In the middle part of the glacier we did not observe any new crevasses exposed by snowmelt, indicating that the lateral crevasses are caused by the progressive detachment of the glacier body. The detected event occurred in years when the mean annual air temperature (MAAT) was above the 46-year trend. No correlation to annual precipitation was found. In this study area, rock and ice avalanches and detachments are not especially sensitive to earthquakes. The catchments DP and SK are made up of redstone, aleurolite, claystone, conglomerates, and limestone. The prevalence of such rocks, which may be easily eroded by glaciers and freeze–thaw processes, is spatially correlated to the particularly high density of surging glaciers present in the area.

impact: Air blast killed 21 people at Everest Base Camp
references: Bartelt et al. (2016); Fujita et al. (2017); Lacroix (2016); Kargel et al. (2015)
comments: Severe Gorkha earthquake (Mw 7.9) released large blocks of ice from a calving glacier located on Pumo Ri Peak (7156 m.a.s.l). The air blast of the powder avalanche killed 21 people. By comparing the satellite imagery before and after the event, the authors were able to identify a 70m * 50m ice mass at 6150 m.a.s.l. This release location is in agreement with eyewitness observations. The release mass was situated on steep terrain (slope angle 55°). The pre- and post-event satellite imagery was used to estimate the release height to be ~10 m, resulting in a total release volume of 53 000m3 of ice. The volume of ice is not large in comparison to other observed ice avalanches in the European Alps. The total volume of the powder cloud was calculated to be >100 * 10^6 m3. Analysis reveals that depletion areas are situated on ice and snow cover. This is also in good agreement with field observations showing that more than half of the deposits in the valley were ice. The total volume depleted by the avalanche is 14.38 ± 0.03 × 10^6 m3. Compared with the 16.61 × 10^6 m3 accumulated, it shows that the deposits gained 15 % in volume during the flow.

impact: Death of 129 Pakistani soldiers and 11 civilian contractors, totaling 140 individuals.
references: Acharya et al. (2023); Landslide Blog; Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: Some experts suggested that a segment of the main glacier might have broken off, leading to the disaster. Others proposed that heavy precipitation could have triggered a landslide comprising boulders, mud, and water. Regular avalanches are uncommon in the Gayari area, which contributed to the base being more extensively developed and housing more personnel than other installations in the Siachen region. The avalanche buried the base under an estimated 21 meters (69 feet) of snow, ice, and rock, covering an area of approximately 1 square kilometer.  The avalanche occurrence clock was advanced by two earthquakes: M 4.1 at a distance ∼ 125 km that occurred about 21 h before and another comparatively larger (M 5.6) earthquake that occurred comparatively at larger distance (∼ 370 km) and longer time (∼ 25 days) before which have significantly changed the loading conditions.

references: van der Woerd et al. (2004)
comments: An avalanche resulted from the collapse of the lower reaches of hanging outlet glacier. The maximum run-out distance was 1 km, and estimates of the volumes of snow and ice 0.15-0.3. Triggered by Mw 7.9 Kokoxili earthquake. Using the classification of Alean (1985), the starting zones for the ice avalanches in the Kunlun Shan are of type TII. Such starting zones are places where the glacier or ice cap develops a near-vertical cliff, typically 30–50 m high, as a result of an abrupt longitudinal change in the slope of the glacier’s bedrock floor. The ice breaks off when the surface becomes too steep or overhangs. In the case of the Kunlun Shan ice avalanches, our observations suggest that the earthquake-induced ground accelerations initiated failures in areas where the slopes on the ice cap were metastable. The ice avalanches in the Kunlun Shan are exceptionally large, with three exceeding 10^6 m3 of transported snow and ice. Only eight other ‘‘pure’’ ice avalanches are known to have exceeded 10^6 m3 in historical time (to the year of 2004).

triggers: Earthquake; Sustained regional warming trend; Meltwater input
impact: Blocked Yarlung Tsangpo River, leading to the inundation of the road to Gyala village
references: Yang et al. (2023); Li et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: The place is famous for many types of catastrophic mass flows: ice avalanches, glacier detachments, debris flows, and ice-rock avalanches from the northern ridge of Gyala Peri in the upper part of the basin. Whilst we do not detect heightened seismic activity around the time of the March 2021 avalanche, it is possible that seismic activity over preceding years and decades may have been a conditioning (rather than triggering) factor. Frequent earthquakes, particularly the M 6.9 earthquake on 18 November 2017 and small-magnitude aftershocks near the Gyala Peri mountain (Zhao et al., 2019), may have enhanced any pre-existing cryospheric instabilities, especially in the high mountain ridges where topographic amplification can occur. Meteorological records from a nearby monitoring station show a significant increase in mean air temperature but an insignificant change in annual total precipitation change. Event of 2021 during an exceptionally warm period outside of the regular summer ablation season. The 2021 avalanche, and previous ones from the basin, occurred concurrently with or shortly after the record of positive air temperature anomalies.

triggers: External mass loading; Earthquake; Precipitation prior to event; Meltwater input; Surge-like activity or surge-type glacier
references: Kääb et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: The place is famous for many types of catastrophic mass flows: ice avalanches, glacier detachments, debris flows, and ice-rock avalanches from the northern ridge of Gyala Peri in the upper part of the basin. It seems very likely that the 22 October 2017 Gyala Peri rock avalanche, which travelled over the Sedongpu Glacier, primed the glacier for its detachment a year later, perhaps with the additional influence of the 18 November 2017 earthquakes. The summer in 2018 was the warmest season during the past four decades; the mean air temperature during June–August was 0.95–1.3 degrees C higher than the historical mean for this period. The effects that the ongoing mass-wasting activities from Gyala Peri had on Sedongpu Glacier could have been manyfold: additional loading on the glacier could have increased normal and shear stresses, and the 2017 rock avalanche and earthquakes could have mechanically weakened the glacier and its bed, potentially disrupting the subglacial drainage system. The large amounts of fine dust deposited on the glacier will likely have changed (enhanced?) its surface melt rates. Lastly, independent factors such as high temperatures and precipitation amounts (Tong et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019) associated with large water input into the glacier could have complicated the changes caused by a rock-avalanche impact. Glacier tongue detached after rapid acceleration, with velocities reaching 25 m/day before failure.

references: Yang et al. (2023); Kääb et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: The place is famous for many types of catastrophic mass flows: ice avalanches, glacier detachments, debris flows, and ice-rock avalanches from the northern ridge of Gyala Peri in the upper part of the basin. The Gyala Peri region, and the southeastern Tibetan Plateau more broadly, are tectonically active. Seismic activity, a known mass movement avalanche trigger, has been proposed as a possible trigger mechanism for avalanche-driven debris flows originating from the Sedongpu valley in 2017 and into 2018 (Zhao et al., 2019).  A huge rock avalanche started high up from the north ridge of Gyala Peri and ran over large parts of the Sedongpu basin and down to Yarlung Tsangpo, damming the river. The event seems to have had a severe impact on Sedongpu Glacier. The avalanche must have changed the surface of Sedongpu Glacier drastically. Then the second event occurred, both events had a total volume of 50 million cubic meters. It covered the glacier and much of the basin with debris and dust. A small, surge-like lobe with ponds on it appeared at the transition between the headwall and the tongue of Sedongpu Glacier. The eastern tributary glacier to Sedongpu Glacier also showed a surge-like lobe.

comments: The place is famous for many types of catastrophic mass flows: ice avalanches, glacier detachments, debris flows, and ice-rock avalanches from the northern ridge of Gyala Peri in the upper part of the basin. This event is classified as possible ice avalanche-induced debris flow. The glacier showed one single tongue in 1969 but had split into two tongues during its advance by 1974, a feature that it still exhibited in 2016. Chen et al. (2020) describe an ice avalanche from the Sedongpu basin that dammed the Yarlung Tsangpo river in 1968. In Corona satellite data of 6 November 1974, the glacier has advanced some 800m into steeper terrain. From Kaab et al., 2021, interpretation of the Corona satellite data there was either one more event between 1969 and 1974, or the event dated “1968” actually happened a few years later.

impact: Blocked Yarlung Tsangpo River and damaged the Zhibai Bridge
references: Yang et al. (2023); Kääb et al. (2021)
comments: Both glacial and fluvial deposits near the outlet of the Zelongnong Valley indicated that this glacier has repeatedly advanced or collapsed since the last glacial maximum (Hu et al., 2020; Montgomery et al., 2004). Four modern glacier collapses have been reported on the Zelongnong Glacier. River blockages have been reported to have occurred in 1950, 1968, and 1984, and the glacier collapse in 1950 engulfed the village of Zhibai and lead to the death of to 97 villagers (Zhang, 1992). In 2020, a total of 1.14 Mm3 of ice-debris mixture produced a high-speed debris flow and partially blocked the Yarlung Tsangpo River and damaged the Zhibai Bridge (Peng et al., 2022).
uncertainties: The process type is uncertain.

impact: Engulfed the village of Zhibai and lead to the death of to 97 villagers
references: Yang et al. (2023); Kääb et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2024)
comments: Four modern glacier collapses have been reported on the Zelongnong Glacier. River blockages have been reported to have occurred in 1950, 1968, and 1984, and the glacier collapse in 1950 engulfed the village of Zhibai and lead to the death of to 97 villagers. Glacier advance rates of up to 1 km/h are reported for the 1950 event (Zhang, 1992). Such rates are far above what is typical for surges, and the glacier might have, at least in 1950, undergone an event close to a sudden detachment in the sense of the present contribution. references: Liu et al. (2022)
comments: Triggered by the earthquake (M 6.8), a small block of fractured ice at the lowest part of icefall collapsed. The magnitude of the coseismic ice avalanche was relatively small, which is comparable in size to most ice avalanches over the past seven years, but much less than the previous mapped largest one (03 April 2018, runout ∼699 m). Hundreds and thousands of ice avalanches, large to small, occur each year at the glacier icefalls in HLG. Some of these medium- to large-scale ice avalanches can be identified by meter-scale remote sensing imagery as they can produce large amounts of ice debris material covering the surface of the (debris-covered) ice tongue below. One most recent large (runout ∼608 m) ice avalanches occurred between 01 and 04 September, just before the earthquake, likely unloaded a large amount of ice mass and making a larger ice avalanche during the earthquake shake.  The entire HLG glacier is just located in a zone with seismic intensity scales between VIII and VII.

impact: Displacement wave caused flooding in Budhi Gandaki River, destroying a wooden bridge and increasing sediment levels
references: Khadka et al. (2025); ICIMOD Website
comments: The melting of both the snow surface and the glacier ice allowed meltwater to seep beneath the crevasses, potentially weakening and destabilising the glacier, leading to the detachment of ice masses or seracs – huge blocks or columns of ice that can topple without warning. We hypothesise that similar phenomena prevailed in this case. According to analysis of the 21 April event, detachment of a massive ice mass from the extensively crevassed part of the glacier snout occurred. This is clearly seen in the textural changes in the PlanetScope satellite images from 19 to 21 April 2024.  The displacement wave created by the huge mass of ice falling into the lake caused the water to overflow, which produced flooding in the immediate downstream area. The evidence from the image showing the number of icebergs floating on the lake water also proves that it was predominantly an avalanche of ice rather than snow, as some initial speculations had suggested. Video Materials are posted on Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/13629302

comments: The earthquake (M 6.4) caused light shaking, assigned IV on the Mercalli intensity scale, but was significant enough to cause a block of serac to detach and tumble down Lenin Peak. The dislodged serac transformed into an avalanche that crashed onto the camp, killing 43 of the 45 climbers. The two survivors, Alexei Koren and Miroslav Brozman, suffered a broken arm and leg. According to them, some team members were still conscious after the avalanche buried them, but rescue attempts failed when the debris hardened into glacier ice. Survivors and witnesses on the mountain did not report any shaking from the earthquake, presumably because the ice acted like a shock absorber. In addition, heavy snowfall occured two days before the tragedy.

triggers: Geothermally induced melting; Meltwater input; Surge-like activity or surge-type glacier; Sustained positive precipitation trend;  Inefficient drainage mechanism
impact: The avalanche travelled 1.7 km in the lake with speed of 200 km per h, generating an impact wave that ran 700–800 m across the flat opposite lake shore with a run-up height of up to 13 m above lake level. Low overall slope angle of 4.9 degrees. No damage occured
references: Kääb et al. (2025)
comments: No lithospheric sediments from the glacier bed were detected, unlike many other low-angle glacier avalanches. The existence of continuously frozen ground around the glacier is confirmed. The development of the Bukadaban glacier detachment is likely the result of a combination of factors and processes, including long-term surge-like motion, polythermal ice, and exceptional warm and wet summer conditions. While the role of frozen glacier margins, and in particular the terminus, is confirmed by the lack of glacier advance and the remaining vertical side wall of the detachment, the relative importance of either surge-like build-up of ice thickness and associated stresses, and summer weather and associated hydrologic and thermal forcing for the acceleration is difficult to decipher.
